sources_considered.why: Primary experimental research directly examines learning and identifies a complete-delegation subgroup.
Read relevant subgroup passages to check methods and interpretation; the paper is represented by the abstract citation rather than counted as another study.
The authors explain contrasting interaction patterns and explicitly limit causal and long-term conclusions.
Search results describe employee surveys and mixed AI use, which do not isolate the all-code delegation condition.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin
evidence_items.explanation: The January research report supports the narrower concern that full delegation can impair learning. Reduced learning relative to a control does not establish zero learning or an inability to improve as an engineer.

evidence_items.locator: Opening summary, paragraph discussing variation in mastery
evidence_items.explanation: Two participants who generated code and then sought explanations showed stronger comprehension, while passive delegation was associated with poorer results. The authors say these subgroup associations are not causal findings and that immediate quiz results do not settle long-term development.

unresolved_gaps: The study does not establish zero learning in the complete-delegation subgroup.
Interaction-pattern subgroups were small and were not independently randomized.
No located evidence establishes the long-term effect of delegating all code writing on broad engineering skill.
The result depends partly on whether active study of generated code falls within the claim.
